prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the accuracy and stability of time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock first after reading the other ballots, and the reason is the shape of the achievement rather than the number of colleagues who placed it high. The discovery is bounded and has a concrete before and after. Katori's magic-wavelength condition lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at optical frequencies without Doppler, recoil or lattice-induced shifts, and Ye's group turned that idea into clocks whose systematic uncertainty and stability reach the 10^-18 level. Several independent laboratories now reproduce and compare these clocks. The consequences reach beyond metrology into centimetre-scale tests of gravitational time dilation, searches for variation of constants and for dark-matter signatures, and a redefinition of the second that is under active discussion. It is also an unusually clean attribution problem: the supplied credit is exactly two people, with the originator of the concept and the person who pushed it to its extreme performance. As a theorist I note that I am drawn to it because it is a clear case of nature being questioned with ever finer tools, in the sense of finding clues in nature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology is the same neighbourhood as the 2005 combs prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems, so the committee could judge the increment to be an improvement in degree rather than a new discovery about nature. Against that, the lattice clock is a distinct invention and not a refinement of ion-trap or comb work, but I cannot fully dismiss the point. A second reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still prospective. A third is that ion-clock pioneers and other strontium and ytterbium lattice groups have claims that the two supplied names do not cover, so the citation must be drawn narrowly around the lattice clock itself.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first, stressing that precision, control and atomic theory (polarisabilities, blackbody shifts) meet cleanly, and flagged an open question whether ion clocks should be recognised alongside it.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and I think her atomic-structure point strengthens it: the magic-wavelength condition and the blackbody shift budget are exactly what make the 10^-18 claim credible. On ion clocks I would resist widening the prize. Folding in Al+ and other ion clocks would add names that exceed three people or force a vaguer citation, and the lattice clock's distinct many-atom advantage is part of what makes it a self-contained achievement. I would take her professional familiarity with the field as a reason to weigh her technical judgement of the systematics heavily, not as a reason to discount it.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the lattice clock is a clean instrument-level invention and that the broader community credit (Hall and Haensch for combs, ion-clock groups) is best handled by framing the citation narrowly.
responses.response: I agree and have written the proposed citation to follow that advice, naming the optical lattice clock rather than optical clocks in general. Where I would add a qualification is that narrow framing protects against the combs overlap but does not remove it: Ye's group relied on comb and ultrastable-laser technology that earlier laureates developed. I think that is acceptable because the lattice clock is a new concept built on that toolkit, but the committee should say so explicitly in the discussion and not assume the point is settled.

responses.point: Pearce ranked the IceCube neutrino discovery first, arguing that the instrument and the physics are inseparable, that the diffuse flux is firmly confirmed, and that this is the kind of discovery the prize has recognised before.
responses.response: This is the most serious competing case for me, and I ranked B041 third. A new observational window is exactly the kind of discovery I regard as central. My reservations are about attribution and about what exactly is credited. IceCube is a very large collaboration that grew out of AMANDA, and with a two-name credit it is difficult to defend that Halzen and Karle alone capture the decisive contributions, whereas for the lattice clock the pairing is natural. The diffuse flux is secure, but the source associations are still statistically less mature. I would not rule out B041 and keep it as an alternative, but I think the lattice clock is the better prize on attribution cleanliness.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked dynamical mean-field theory first, as a conceptually clear and widely used framework for correlated electrons, while acknowledging that Metzner is missing from the supplied credit.
responses.response: I respect the originality and the three decades of use, and as a theorist I find the infinite-dimension limit elegant. My concern is the same one he raises himself: Metzner's role in the 1989 limit is not in the credited names, so a trio of Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt cannot be treated as fair without a decision we cannot make from this list. The distinction between rewarding a method and rewarding a discovery also matters to me. I would need a clearer answer on attribution before supporting it over a case with a clean two-person credit.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as the architecture behind most superconducting processors, while noting that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits sits very close and that credited names omit some co-authors.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is original and extremely influential. I ranked it fifth mainly because of the proximity to the 2025 prize, which he himself raises, and because the credit among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf omits Girvin and others who were part of the architecture. I also value his candour about a possible perceived conflict from his own field. I think the committee would be wise to wait a few years before returning to superconducting circuits, whereas the lattice clock has no such recent neighbour.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 combs prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize.
Whether ion clocks or other lattice-clock groups deserve a share that the two supplied names do not provide.

Whether topological insulators (B057) should outrank the lattice clock given the unresolved credit for the HgTe proposal and the 2016 overlap; I currently judge that attribution problem to be the deciding difference.
Whether the large-collaboration credit problem for IceCube (B041) can be resolved in a two-name prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none of them is connected to any shortlisted candidate or credited name that I am aware of.
